newsitem.title: UK: Shorts says couldn't stay in limbo over Fokker.
newsitem.headline: Shorts says couldn't stay in limbo over Fokker.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Short Brothers Plc, which dashed hopes of a rescue for Fokker by refusing to supply its wings, said on Thursday it had been reluctant to stay in limbo awaiting a decision on the Dutch planemaker's future.
Fokker, one of the great names in pioneering aviation history, was declared bankrupt in March after racking up huge losses, but had limped on in the hope of a last-minute rescue.

As Dutch, Russian and Canadian suitors decided not to take on Fokker, thousands of skilled workers left, deadlines came and went and hopes of salvaging something from Fokker's wreckage rested on takeover talks with South Korea's Samsung Aerospace.
But on Thursday, Samsung told the Dutch government, a minority Fokker shareholder, that it needed another month before being able to decide whether or not to take Fokker over.
That was the final straw for Belfast-based Shorts, a subsidiary of Canadian planemaker Bombardier, which makes the wings for Fokker F-70 and F-100 regional jets.
Shorts said it would no longer supply wings to Fokker, prompting Fokker's administrators to say that a relaunch of the company would no longer be feasible.

"We had to be able to get on with our future," a spokesman for Shorts said. "Samsung seemed unable to reach a decision with its partners and the South Korean government and in the end suppliers like ourselves had to say enough is enough."

"We lost nearly 1,000 jobs with the collapse of Fokker and our main factory has lain idle for nine months," he told Reuters. "We will now be able to get on with our future and install on our production lines new work that we are winning."

The spokesman said Shorts had told Fokker's administrators that although it was no longer willing to do the final assembly of wings for Fokker, it was still willing to help in "all other ways," such as offering technical expertise and aiding the transfer of production of the wings to another source.

"We very much regret that the trustees decided not to proceed with discussions to transfer production elsewhere," he said. Shorts said it had already won new business since the collapse of Fokker and was in negotiations to secure more.

"Within three or four years we hope to have won enough business to replace the business lost over Fokker," the spokesman said. "In the last few months we have started to recruit people again, and prospects for the future look good."
